newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU ministers agree ERM II will maintain wide bands - SEP 21.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers agree ERM II will maintain wide bands - SEP 21.

text.p: EU finance ministers agreed on Saturday that a new Exchange Rate Mechanism to be set up after the launch of the single European currency in 1999 will keep the wide fluctuation bands of the current system, officials said.
The new mechanism, the ERM II, will limit fluctuations between the euro and currencies whose countries are waiting to join European monetary union when their economies are ready.
"There is a consensus to maintain the relatively wide bands of today," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters.

The European Union was forced to widen the fluctuation bands of the existing exchange rate mechanism to plus or minus 15 percent of a central rate from 2.25 percent after a currency crisis in the summer of 1993.
One delegation source said ministers had been asked whether they had any objection to maintaining the current system after the launch of the euro, and none had objected.
"My reading of that is that it will be plus or minus 15 percent," the source said.

A European Commission spokesman said no-one had asked for bands less than 15 percent, though narrower bands were possible for countries with economies which were closely aligned to those of the euro zone.
One source said details still had to be ironed out on how to set up these narrower bands, and ministers declined to confirm the new system would retain the precise limit of 15 percent.

"We have not finalised the bands for ERM II. We have asked for additional work to be done. We want some more clarity on how it is going to function and ensure that the new ERM will work efficiently," Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said.

Commission officials also hinted countries still outside European monetary union which failed to follow sensible monetary and fiscal policies could lose the support of the future European Central Bank (ECB) if their currencies came under pressure on exchange markets.
That would mean the ECB might either stop intervening to support those currencies or it would suggest a devaluation.
"There may be an implicit deal between respect of economic programmes in the (convergence) plan and membership of the ERM II," a Commission spokesman said.
The new exchange rate mechanism will be based on the euro, with the exchange rates of countries waiting to join monetary union, the "pre-ins", fixed against it.
"The new system will be a system of hubs and spokes, with the euro in the centre and fairly wide bands around," the spokesman said.
The ECB would intervene to defend these currencies if necessary, but would be able to stop intervention in certain circumstances.
"The European Central Bank and the central banks of the pre-ins can stop intervention if it would endanger the central goal which is the stability of prices," the spokesman said.

European Monetary Institute head Alexandre Lamfalussy, in a confidential letter written earlier this month, a copy of which was circulating at the talks, recommended that the ECB would have the right to initiate procedures aimed at realigning currencies in ERM II if necessary.
